text: Complacency is the comfortable feeling that a problem is already handled, and the lowering of your guard that follows it. The word always carries a criticism: nobody praises complacency, they warn about it, because the danger is the effort you stop making while you feel pleased with yourself. Having just argued that democracies survived far worse violence in the 1970s and 80s, the writer heads off the wrong lesson — surviving the past is not evidence that today is safe.

Tawdry means cheap and showy in a way that leaves a grubby impression — it started as a word for flashy junk jewellery and kept that flavour of glitter that fails a close look. Applied to people and their dealings it means sordid and undignified: a tawdry scandal, a tawdry deal. The process the writer calls tawdry is ordinary politics, the deal-making and the handing out of public money, and admitting it looks grubby is the setup for his real point: grubby beats extremists killing for a cause.

A zealot is someone whose devotion to a cause has gone past the point of reason — no weighing of evidence, no compromise, no possibility of being wrong. The name comes from the Zealots, a Jewish faction that fought Roman rule in the first century, and it keeps that edge of dangerous commitment, which is why calling someone a zealot is an accusation while zealous can simply mean eager. Here it describes the hard-line communists who had captured European labour unions, running them for a coming revolution rather than for their members.

To weather something is to come through it and still be standing — you weather a storm, a scandal, a bad season. It has nothing to do with the forecast here, though the image comes from the same place: the thing beats on you and you endure it. The subtitle's claim is that open societies have already survived murderous extremists of both the left and the right.

When something looms, it is coming and it feels threatening — a deadline looms, a storm looms, exams loom. The word suggests a large shape rising up ahead of you, so it is never used for good news. Saying that ugly elections loom in America, Brazil, France and Israel sets the article's anxious opening note.

A peddler once walked from village to village selling small goods, so to peddle is to hawk something, pushing it on whoever will take it. Applied to ideas rather than objects it becomes an insult: you peddle rumours, conspiracy theories, get-rich-quick schemes. Candidates peddling impossible promises are selling voters something they cannot deliver.

To sow is to scatter seed across a field, and almost every use you meet in journalism is the figurative one: you sow doubt, confusion, division, the seeds of something that grows later. It is pronounced like so, not like the female pig spelled the same way. Foreign governments using fake videos and bots to sow distrust are planting suspicion and letting it spread on its own.

A rogue is a dishonest, unprincipled operator — in older English a likeable scoundrel, in politics something harder. Governments that break international rules are routinely called rogue states, and going rogue means acting outside the rules you are supposed to follow. Russia and other rogues means states that behave as outlaws rather than as members in good standing.

A saboteur is someone who deliberately wrecks or disrupts something from within — machinery, a supply line, a plan, an election. The word is French and keeps its French shape and sound, sab-uh-TUR, with sabotage the noun for the act. Hiring saboteurs to spread fear means paying people to cause trouble inside another country's election.

Newfangled means newly invented, said with a raised eyebrow — the speaker is not sure the new thing is an improvement. It is an old, slightly mocking word usually aimed at gadgets and fashions. Calling AI-powered videos and bots newfangled attacks sets them against the old-fashioned ones the article goes on to describe: bombs, guns and kidnappings.

To be vigilant is to stay alert for danger, watching steadily rather than reacting in panic. It shares a root with vigil, sitting awake through the night, and the related noun is vigilance. The advice that voters be vigilant but hold their nerve pairs watchfulness with calm, which is the whole argument of the piece in six words.

Effete describes something that has lost its strength and become soft, overrefined and useless — originally said of soil worn out by farming. It is a put-down aimed at people or institutions thought too delicate to survive rough treatment. Saying democracy is not an effete or genteel pastime insists it is built for conflict, not for polite occasions.

Genteel means refined and well-mannered in a slightly fussy, old-fashioned way, and it is usually faintly mocking — a genteel tea party, genteel poverty that hides behind good manners. It is related to gentle and gentleman rather than to genuine. Paired with effete, it makes democracy sound like a hobby for delicate people, which is the idea the writer is about to knock down.

To channel something is to dig it a path and make it flow where you want, the way a canal directs water instead of letting a flood spread. Used of feelings it means putting the energy to work rather than suppressing it: channelling anger into training. The genius of free societies is to channel fury into politics — the rage is not removed, it is given somewhere to go.

Here genius does not mean a brilliant person but the defining brilliance of a thing — the clever quality that makes it work, as in the genius of the design. This is the older sense, a spirit or character belonging to something. The genius of free societies is a talent the system has, not a talent anyone in it possesses.

A grievance is a complaint about being treated unfairly, felt strongly enough to demand a remedy — workers file grievances, groups nurse historical ones. It is related to grieve, and it carries the sense of an injury that has not been put right. Managing conflicts and grievances through debate and public money is the article's picture of politics doing its job.

Watch the sense here: liable to means likely to, with a hint that it is the kind of thing this person tends to do. That is different from liable on its own in law, which means legally responsible and on the hook to pay. Le Pen described as liable to dismantle much of Macron's legacy means she can be expected to do it, not that anyone could sue her for it.

To scrutinise something is to examine it closely and sceptically, looking for what a quick glance would miss; the noun is scrutiny. The article spells it with an s because The Economist is British; American writing uses scrutinizing. Scrutinising decades of police and press reports is how the researchers arrived at their counts of bombings and killings.

In news writing domestic means inside the country's own borders, the opposite of foreign — domestic flights, domestic politics, a domestic market. The household sense you know from domestic chores is a different use of the same word. The article's key statistic depends on the distinction: foreign terrorists killed many Italians, but domestic political violence killed even more.

To thwart someone is to block what they are trying to do so it fails — a plan is thwarted, an attack is thwarted, an ambition is thwarted. The word implies frustration, an effort stopped just short of success. Moro thwarted the Red Brigades by drawing communists into government, which removed the grievance a revolution needed.

A lift in British English is an elevator, so stopping a lift between floors means trapping the box halfway up the shaft where nobody can interrupt. The police commander does it to speak privately for a few seconds. British usage runs through this piece — favour, scrutinising, labour — because The Economist is published in London.

To shield someone is to hold something between them and harm, and in politics it usually means covering for a wrongdoer so investigators cannot reach them. The word makes the protection deliberate rather than accidental. Elected politicians shielding extremists is the article's most disturbing claim about the era: the state's own people were protecting the killers.

To straddle is to stand with a leg on each side of something — a fence, a horse, a border — and figuratively to belong to two categories at once. A company straddling two industries fits neatly in neither. Islamist terrorism straddling ideology and religious hatred means it is driven by politics and by faith together, so explaining it with only one of the two misses it.

A scourge was a whip used for punishment, and the word now names any widespread affliction that keeps hurting people — the scourge of malaria, of drink-driving, of online scams. It is stronger than problem and implies suffering inflicted again and again. Calling Islamist terrorism a scourge places it with the lasting plagues rather than the passing troubles.

An ideology is a complete system of political ideas that tells its holders how the world works and what should be done about it — communism, fascism, liberalism. Because it explains everything, an ideology can justify anything, which is why the word often appears near violence. The article separates the world of ideology from the world of religious hatred, then says Islamist terrorism sits in both.

Something sobering makes you serious and quiet, knocking the cheerfulness out of you the way cold water might — a sobering statistic, a sobering thought. It borrows the image of becoming sober, but nothing about drink is meant. The political scientists' sobering reply is the unwelcome answer that America, with its armed protesters and militias, is a case apart.

To forgo something is to give it up or do without it, usually something you were entitled to — forgoing a salary, forgoing dessert, forgoing your turn. Note the spelling: forgo means go without, while forego with an e means go before, as in the foregoing paragraph. A state forgoing its legal monopoly over violence is surrendering a power it is entitled to keep.

Consequential means important because of the consequences it has — a consequential decision changes what happens next, and a consequential president leaves the country altered. It is the opposite of inconsequential, which is the more common word. Trump's remark that only consequential presidents get shot at turns being a target into a compliment.

As an adjective grave means serious and threatening — grave dangers, a grave error, a grave illness — and it can also describe a solemn face. It has nothing to do with the noun for a burial place, though both come from ideas of weight and heaviness. Saying democracy faces grave dangers keeps the warning in place even as the writer urges confidence.

A demagogue is a leader who wins power by whipping up people's fears and resentments rather than by argument, usually by naming an enemy to blame. The word is Greek for leader of the people and has been an insult since ancient Athens, where such leaders were blamed for wrecking the city's democracy. A sinister demagogue of the right is one half of the bad choice the article imagines voters facing in a run-off.

A guerrilla is a fighter in a small irregular force that avoids open battle, using ambushes and raids against a much larger army. The word is Spanish for little war, and it is pronounced like gorilla, which is a different animal entirely. Che Guevara, the Argentine doctor who fought in Cuba's revolution, is the most famous example, and his face on posters and T-shirts is why Western students in the 1970s took him as a model.

A regime is a government, named that way when the writer wants to stress that it rules rather than that it was chosen — you rarely hear a democracy called a regime. It can also mean an established system of rules, as in a trade regime or an exercise regime. Chairman Mao's revolutionary regime in China is the model some Western students admired, at the time it was killing millions of its own citizens.

To hold your nerve is to stay steady under pressure when the tempting thing is to panic, back out, or do something rash. It is what commentators say about a penalty taker, a negotiator, or an investor in a falling market. Voters holding their nerve means not abandoning the system because an election looks frightening.

A sore loser cannot accept losing gracefully, complaining that the game was rigged or the referee was blind. The sore means resentful and bruised, not physically painful. In an election the sore loser is a serious matter rather than a playground annoyance, because questioning the result, as the article says, casts doubt on the integrity of the whole vote.

Horse-trading is hard, shrewd bargaining in which each side gives something to get something, from the old reputation of horse dealers for driving a sharp deal. In politics it is the swapping of votes, favours and budget lines that turns a disagreement into a law. The article calls parliamentary horse-trading a tool, one of the ways an angry conflict gets settled with deals instead of bombs.

To tally something up is to count it item by item and reach a total, and a tally is the running count — the word comes from the notched sticks once used to keep score. It suggests patient adding rather than an estimate. The researchers tallied up 1,802 bombings and 716 arson attacks, which is why those numbers carry weight.

To reject one thing in favour of another is to choose the second instead of the first, so the phrase marks a swap, not just an opinion. Spelled favor in American English; the u is British. Students who scorned democracy in favour of class struggle traded one political idea for another, and the article thinks they chose badly.

To be bent on something is to be set on it with a determination that will not be talked out of, and it is nearly always used for something harmful — bent on revenge, bent on destruction. The image is of a person leaning hard in one direction. Revolutionaries bent on destroying the state were not open to persuasion, which is what made sympathy for them so dangerous.

The moral of a story is the lesson you are meant to take from it — the line at the end of a fable. Used this way it is a noun and has nothing to do with being moral in the sense of good behaviour. Saying the moral is clear announces the article's conclusion: keep politics open, because shutting it down pushes rage into the streets.

To play out is to unfold to its end, the way a game or an argument runs its course once it has begun — we will see how it plays out. It implies the ending is not yet settled. Conflicts that cannot play out in election campaigns and parliaments have nowhere to finish, which is the article's explanation for political violence.

The Years of Lead is what Italians call the period from roughly 1969 to 1988, when far-left and far-right groups tried to destroy the Italian state with bombings, shootings and kidnappings. Lead means bullets. The researchers quoted here counted 1,802 bombings, 716 arson attacks and 98 knee-cappings in those years, killing 530 people, and the whole article is an argument from that history to the present.

The Red Brigades were an Italian far-left terrorist group founded around 1970 that aimed to overthrow the state and pull Italy out of its Western alliances. Red is the traditional colour of communism. Their most notorious act was the 1978 kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro, and their logic is the article's central exhibit: they killed the politician who was making revolution unnecessary.

Aldo Moro was one of Italy's dominant post-war politicians, prime minister five times, and the architect of an opening to the country's large Communist Party. The Red Brigades held him for 55 days in 1978, staged what they called a people's trial, and shot him. His death is the article's measure of how much worse politics has been than it is now.

A run-off is a second round of voting between the top two candidates, held because nobody won a majority the first time — France elects its president this way. It guarantees the winner is backed by more than half of those who turn out, but it can leave voters with two candidates they dislike. That is the trap the article describes: a run-off between a demagogue of the right and a populist of the left.

In a coalition government two or more parties agree to govern together because none of them won enough seats to command a majority alone, voting as a bloc and dividing the ministries between them. The smaller partner's price is policy, and the government falls if it walks out. Moro was building one, bringing Italy's Communists toward power by election rather than revolution, and the Red Brigades killed him for it.

A populist politician frames politics as the pure ordinary people against a corrupt elite, and claims to speak for the people directly. Populists exist on the left and the right, which is why the article can put an irresponsible populist of the left opposite a demagogue of the right. The label is usually applied by critics rather than chosen.

A centrist sits in the middle of the political spectrum, between the left and the right, generally favouring gradual change and existing institutions. Macron and Merz are the article's examples, and its point is how unloved they are — one facing replacement by a nationalist, the other polling at 13%. Centrist leaders do have grounds for gloom is the article conceding its opponents' strongest point before answering it.

The chancellor is Germany's head of government, the equivalent of a prime minister, chosen by parliament rather than elected directly by voters. Germany's president is a separate and largely ceremonial job. Friedrich Merz holding the post with 13% approval is the article's joke about bank-robbers being more popular.

A parliament is the assembly that makes a country's laws, and in most democracies it also chooses the government, so the prime minister stays in office only while parliament keeps supporting them. That is the difference from the American system, where a president is elected separately from Congress and cannot be voted out by it. Parliamentary horse-trading is the bargaining between parties inside such an assembly.

Political scientists describe the state as holding a monopoly over violence: only the government may legally use force, arresting, imprisoning or deploying armed men, and everyone else is barred from it. That is why the same acts committed privately are kidnapping, theft and murder. Tolerating armed protesters and militias means forgoing part of that monopoly, which is the article's explanation for why America is a case apart.

A militia is an armed group of civilians organised outside the regular army, sometimes officially, often not. The problem the article points to is the unofficial kind: private citizens with weapons and a command structure, ready to act on their own political judgment. Where militias operate openly and unchallenged, the state is no longer the only body able to use force.

A separatist wants their region to break away and become its own country, or to join a neighbouring one. It is a distinct motive from left-wing or right-wing revolution, which is why the article lists separatist groups separately: the IRA sought a united Ireland, ETA an independent Basque country. The article's hopeful point is that separatists were eventually drawn into legal parties and elections.

The IRA, the Irish Republican Army, was a paramilitary group that fought to end British rule in Northern Ireland and unite it with the Irish republic, killing and bombing for decades. It came close to killing Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in a 1984 hotel bombing. Its campaign ended through negotiation, with its political wing entering ordinary elected politics.

Baader-Meinhof is the popular name for West Germany's Red Army Faction, a far-left group of the 1970s and 80s that killed bankers, industrialists and officials in the hope of provoking a revolution. It was named after two of its founders. Along with November 17 in Greece, it is the article's evidence that Italy's Years of Lead were not an Italian peculiarity.

Class struggle is the Marxist idea that history is driven by conflict between the class that owns factories and land and the class that has only its labour to sell, and that this fight must end in revolution. Choosing it over democracy means deciding that elections cannot deliver justice and only a seizure of power will. That is exactly the choice the article says a dismaying number of Western students and intellectuals made.

A trade union is an organisation of workers that bargains with employers over pay and conditions, and can call a strike to back its demands; Americans usually say labor union. Its ordinary business is wages, not revolution. The article's complaint is that some European unions had been captured by hard-line communists, which is why strikes peaked in the 1960s even as workers were getting steadily richer.

Stalinists and Trotskyites were rival kinds of communist, divided by the 1920s fight between Joseph Stalin, who took control of the Soviet Union, and Leon Trotsky, whom he exiled and had murdered. Stalinists backed the Soviet state as it was; Trotskyites accused it of betraying the revolution and called for a worldwide one. The bitterness between them is the source of the phrase that the far left fights the far left hardest.

Islamist is a political word, not a religious one: it describes movements that want the state itself governed by Islamic law, and a small violent fringe of them use terrorism to pursue it. It is not a synonym for Islamic or Muslim, which describe a faith and the people who hold it. The distinction is why the article can call Islamist terrorism a scourge straddling ideology and religious hatred.

A ballot is a vote, and the ballot box is the sealed container voters drop their marked papers into, so the phrase stands for elections themselves. Ballot boxes can beat bullets is the article's closing line and its whole argument compressed: conflicts settled by counting votes instead of by killing. The rhyme is doing work, but the claim underneath it is the historical one the piece spent 900 words making.
